title: Tip-Tuned Renormalization-Group Spectroscopy Unmasks a False-positive Topological Superconducting Vortex
authors: Zhenhua Zhu, Qun Zhu, Yong-Wei Wang, Gu Zhang, Jihai Zhang, Xu-Cun Ma, Qi-Kun Xue, Can-Li Song, Dong E. Liu
abstract: Clean, nonsplit vortex zero-bias peaks (ZBPs) can be misinterpreted as Majorana zero modes (MZMs), making static scanning tunneling microscopy intrinsically ambiguous. Here we use the STM tip coupling to drive a local boundary-renormalization-group (boundary RG) flow, turning dynamical Coulomb blockade into a falsification test for Majorana-like ZBPs. Experimentally, in a $\mathrm{SrSn}_3$ thin film, normal-state spectra establish an Ohmic dissipative environment, and a common boundary-RG/thermodynamic-Bethe-ansatz analysis of the superconducting-gap and vortex-center spectra yields consistent dissipation strengths within the $r < 1/2$ Majorana-filter regime. Lowering the tip nevertheless drives a clean, non-split vortex-center ZBP into a zero-bias dip, opposite to the protected flow of an isolated MZM, unmasking the peak as a Majorana false positive produced by a conventional vortex-core state. The same flow selectively suppresses the strongly tip-coupled channel, resolving the two-gap superconductivity. Dissipative STM thus tests dynamical protection rather than spectral appearance.
summary: The authors developed a novel spectroscopic technique using tip-height tuning within the boundary Renormalization Group framework to probe vortex cores in superconductors. They successfully used this method to distinguish between true Majorana zero modes and trivial resonances by observing that the characteristic flow of the ZBP contradicted MZM theory, proving the peak was a false positive.
main_problem: The primary challenge is distinguishing between true topological superconducting vortex states, which host Majorana zero modes (MZMs), and false positive zero-bias conductance peaks (ZBPs) arising from conventional vortex cores using STM.
main_result: By analyzing the dynamical evolution of the ZBP as the tip coupling is tuned via boundary renormalization group flow, the authors demonstrated that the observed peak was a non-topological feature whose flow contradicted MZM predictions.
method: The study combines low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) measurements with advanced theoretical modeling using boundary Renormalization Group (RG) theory and the Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) to analyze dissipative quantum circuits.
model_or_system: The experiment is performed on $	ext{SrSn}_3$ thin films, treating the STM junction as a local probe coupled to an Ohmic environment. The physics is modeled using concepts from boundary RG flow applied to superconducting vortex cores and tunneling barriers.
key_observables: Zero-bias conductance peak (ZBP) evolution; dissipation strength ($r$); spectral weight fitting across single-channel, two-channel SC gap, and high-field regimes.
important_parameters: Dissipation strength $r < 1/2$; tip coupling parameter tuning the boundary RG flow; superconducting gap parameters ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the low-energy spectral evolution is governed by a universal dissipative environment response derived from TBA, allowing for the separation of trivial and topological contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup (STM junction in a dissipative environment) and show the critical diagnostic: how lowering the tip drives an initial ZBP into a zero-bias dip, which is contrasted with theoretical MZM flow predictions. Other figures detail global fits across various spectral components.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the ambiguity of static ZBPs, introduces the boundary RG/TBA framework to test dynamical protection, applies this method to $	ext{SrSn}_3$ vortex spectra, and concludes by showing that the observed flow pattern definitively rules out an MZM interpretation for the measured peak.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful experimental methodology—using controlled environmental coupling (dissipative STM)—to perform dynamical quantum state verification, moving beyond simple spectral measurements to test fundamental topological protection in superconducting systems.
